citation: Garthe I, Raastad T, Refsnes PE, Koivisto A, Sundgot-Borgen J. Effect of Two Different Weight-Loss Rates on Body Composition and Strength and Power-Related Performance in Elite Athletes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2011;21(2):97-104.
groupLabel: Slow reduction (SR), 0.7% body weight/week target
energyPrescription: Individualized diet aimed at 0.7% body-weight loss per week; ~19% reduction in energy intake vs. estimated requirement; low fat (~20% of energy); 4 supervised resistance-training sessions/week.
cardioDescription: Normal sport-specific training continued; no additional cardio prescribed.
notes: Abstract reports only percent changes (BW -5.6%, FM -31%, LBM +2.1%); kg values solved algebraically from those plus baseline weight 71.9 kg. Elite athletes GAINED 1.16 kg lean in a sustained ~19% deficit; engine's MUSCLE_SITUATION gives elite=0.00 above a 15% deficit, so it predicts exactly zero lean gain.

citation: Garthe I, et al. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2011;21(2):97-104.
groupLabel: Fast reduction (FR), 1.4% body weight/week target
energyPrescription: Individualized diet aimed at 1.4% body-weight loss per week; ~30% energy reduction; 4 supervised RT sessions/week.
cardioDescription: Normal sport-specific training continued.
notes: Reported: BW -5.5%, FM -21%, LBM -0.2% (n.s.). The real penalty of the fast arm showed up as FORGONE lean gain (+1.16 SR vs -0.11 FR = 1.27 kg swing), not as absolute loss. The engine models it through leanLossPerWeek() only.

citation: Kistler BM, Fitschen PJ, Ranadive SM, Fernhall B, Wilund KR. Case Study: Natural Bodybuilding Contest Preparation. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2014;24(6):694-700.

cardioDescription: Cardiovascular training progressively INCREASED across 26 weeks.
notes: Verified: 88.6 -> 73.3 kg, 17.5% -> 7.4% BF. Reviews quote 6.6 kg FFM loss (DXA lean soft tissue) vs my 5.2 kg derivation; use 5.2-6.6 as a range. 0.20-0.25 kg lean/wk for 26 wk at only ~14% deficit.

citation: Campbell BI, et al. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2018;28(6):580-585.

citation: Hatamoto Y, et al. Greater energy surplus promotes body protein accretion in healthy young men: A randomized clinical trial. Clinical Nutrition 2024;43:48-60.
groupLabel: P group — +10% energy surplus from protein alone (ITT, n=12)
energyPrescription: Fully provided diet equal to measured energy requirement plus whey equal to +10% of requirement. Achieved 2.3 g/kg BW/d protein.
cardioDescription: No exercise prescribed; free-living activity monitored by accelerometer and DLW
notes: NO RESISTANCE TRAINING — a pure overfeeding trial that bounds what a surplus alone does. Total body protein mass change was 0.00 +/- 0.61 kg, so the FFM gain was water/glycogen. Implied lean fraction 0.83.
leanScoringBasis: body protein mass change (0.00 +/- 0.61 kg), NOT 4C fat-free mass (+0.73 kg). The 4C FFM gain was water/glycogen; scoring the engine against it would tune muscle to hydration.

citation: Hatamoto Y, et al. Clinical Nutrition 2024;43:48-60.
groupLabel: PE group — +40% energy surplus (+10% protein, +30% CHO) (ITT, n=11)
energyPrescription: Requirement + protein supplement (+10%) + carbohydrate supplement (+30%). Achieved 2.2 g/kg BW/d protein.
cardioDescription: No exercise prescribed.
notes: Protein mass +0.44 +/- 0.34 kg (p=0.003). Implied lean fraction 0.53. vs the +10% arm: FFM gain roughly doubled but FAT gain rose ~8x for a 4x larger surplus. Cleanest available test of how fat gain should scale with surplus size.
leanScoringBasis: body protein mass change (+0.44 +/- 0.34 kg, p=0.003), NOT 4C fat-free mass (+1.31 kg).

citation: Antonio J, et al. JISSN 2016;13:3.
groupLabel: High-protein condition >3 g/kg/d (8-week period of a 16-week crossover), n=12 men
energyPrescription: High-protein diet >3 g/kg/d. Achieved 3.3 g/kg/d protein and 2903 kcal/d.

inferredFields: deltaLeanMassKg (computed by me from crossover condition means)
notes: Eating ~450 kcal/d MORE than baseline for 8 weeks produced a LOWER body weight and lower fat mass with unchanged FFM. No differences reached significance. Direct evidence against a naive kcal-in/kcal-out fat-gain model for high-protein surpluses, but self-reported intake is the weak link.
